items.note: The Udaipur praśasti gives 'a complete and exhaustive genealogy' of the Paramāra house down to Udayāditya; undated, purpose not shown, intended to be put in a part of the temple.

claim.value: undated; complete Paramāra genealogy to Udayāditya; praśasti for a temple

items.note: Language Sanskrit, wholly metrical apart from an opening obeisance to Śiva; twenty-two verses survive, the next verse breaking off after ten aksharas.
Four maṅgala-ślokas: two to Śiva, then Pārvatī and Gaṇeśa, whose invocation occurs here for the first time in an inscription of this house.
Praśasti verses 5-6: hero sprung from Vasishtha's fire-altar on Mount Arbuda receives the name Paramāra; editor calls it 'purely legendary, a later creation', first mentioned in this inscription.
Verse 8 names Upēndrarāja as first Paramāra king of Mālwā; land grants name Krishnarāja, taken by Hall, Cunningham and Bühler as the same.
Verses 8-11 name Vairisinha, Siyaka, Vākpati and a second Vairisinha (Vajraṭa); the only record giving a complete genealogy of the earlier Paramāra rulers.
Verses 13-15 praise Vākpati (Muñja) as versed in the Śāstras and a poet; known by other names in other records.

Praśasti claims Vākpati's victories over Karnāṭas, Lāṭas, Keralas, Cholas and the Kalachuri Yuvarāja; editor finds the Karnāṭa claim 'evidently inadmissible' and lacks evidence for the Yuvarāja clash.
From Mērutuṅga: Vākpati taken prisoner and killed by Tailapa after crossing the Godāvarī; event placed between 993-94 and 997-98 A.C.
Sindhurāja, Vākpati's younger brother, victorious over a king of the Hūnas; the Navasāhasāṅka-charita adds further victories.
Sindhurāja must have reigned into the first decade of the eleventh century, closing before 1011 A.C., earliest date of Bhōja.
Praśasti vv. 16-20 eulogise Bhōja for strength, charities, victories and temple building; kavirāja title; enemies listed; the sweeping claims are called 'merely a poetic way of expression'.
Verse 20 says Bhōja 'covered the world all around with temples' of Kēdāra, Rāmēśvara, Sōmanātha and others; Bühler remarks it cannot be corroborated.
Bhōja's earliest epigraphic date is the Mōdāsā grant of V.S. 1067 or 1011 A.C.
Bhōja's latest known date is the Tilakawādā grant of V.S. 1103 or 1047 A.C.
Verse 21 introduces Udayāditya as 'another Sun'; after Kalachuri Karṇa and Chaulukya Bhīma took Bhōja's kingdom, the Nagpur praśasti says Udayāditya delivered the earth like the Great Boar.
Credit of vanquishing Karṇa, Bhīma and Ereyāṅga goes to Udayāditya, 'who was his brother, as the Dōngargāon inscription informs us'.
Bühler doubts the story of Bhōja's reverse; editor cites the 'total destruction' of the Kalachuri king by Udayāditya, and verse 22 hints at restoration of a Boar-temple by Udayāditya.

items.note: Three Anushṭubh stanzas dedicate the Varṇa-nāga-kṛipāṇikā (alphabetical snake-scimitar) to Udayāditya and Naravarman; prāsasti presumably composed by Naravarman.
Nāgari alphabet engraved class-wise after the praśasti with totals for each group (14 vowels, 2 anusvāra/visarga, consonants ka to ha totalling 51).
Long vowels and the Māhēśvara-sūtras follow, with total of 47 letters and sub-totals for each group.
Varṇanāga-kṛipāṇikā: a scimitar formed from letters and a snake; head engraved with the fourteen vowels, body with ha, ya, va, ra, la and 25 squares of sparśa consonants.
